newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim makes ultimate sacrifice - his son.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim makes ultimate sacrifice - his son.

text.p: He has given up jogging, his golf game and even his old friendships, but the sacrifice that South Korea's Kim Young-sam is now making for the sake of his presidency has reached a new scale.
As he fights for survival in a bribery scandal, Kim has been forced to turn his back on his own son, who is accused of taking kickbacks.

In an agonised television address, Kim made clear last February justice would have to take its course if his son was implicated in the scandal involving billions of dollars of loans to a failed steelmaker.
Now Kim Hyun-chul, 38, has been thrown into a feeding frenzy involving state prosecutors, lawmakers in the National Assembly and the media.
An arrest is imminent, and by the end of Kim Young-sam's single term next February -- if he lasts that long -- the young Kim could be behind bars.
"It's not really a sacrifice," said Moon Chung-in, a professor of politics at Yonsei University. "It is the only logical thing to do."
"Trying to save Kim Hyun-chul would be a disaster for everyone."

Kim Hyun-chul, in the minds of many South Koreans, embodies the failures of his father's presidency, which started out full of hope for reforming a corrupt society but which is now wallowing in a tide of sleaze.
Several of the president's closest aides are on trial for their roles in the scandal over loans to Hanbo Steel Co, which collapsed in January with debts of US$5.8 billion.

The president is so badly wounded that when he recently "vowed to do my best until the very end of my term", his words were widely interpreted as a response to spreading rumours he might be compelled to step down early.

An announcement last month that Kim Young-sam was giving up his morning jog was seized upon by commentators as another sign of exhaustion and defeat. A spokesman said Kim was following doctor's orders.
When he took office, Kim stopped playing golf as an unnecessary extravagence -- and instructed his Blue House aides to pack away their golf clubs too.
In the South Korean tradition of aloof Confucian leadership, Kim virtually withdrew from society and stopped seeing old friends and associates.
Without his son -- who helped engineer his 1992 election victory, and quickly became dubbed the "crown prince" -- Kim Young-sam is more isolated than ever.
"The nation is like a rudderless, drifting boat," the Chosun Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial.

At an annual prayer breakfast at Seoul's Hilton Hotel two weeks ago, Kim Young-sam revealed that he knelt in prayer twice each day to seek healing for the country. His own presidency may be beyond repair.
Already, powerful figures in his ruling New Korea Party are jockeying to become the party's candidate in December's presidential elections.
And his abilty to influence the succession has been impaired by the bribery scandal, whose leading casualties have been members of a party faction of Kim Young-sam loyalists.
In a further blow, opposition parties are demanding Kim Young-sam present a full accounting of his spending on the 1992 election, alleging he far exceeded legal expenditure limits.
If his son goes to jail, said Moon, the Yonsei University professor, Kim Young-sam would not be able to pardon him before he left office. To do so would be to invite a new storm of criticism.
"Any pardon would have to come from his successor," said Moon.
